title: Kadic v. Karadzic
citation: 70 F.3d 232 (2d Cir. 1995), rehearing denied, 74 F.3d 377 (2d Cir. 1996)
lead: Victims alleging atrocities in Bosnia sued a Bosnian-Serb leader during his New York visits. The court recognized jurisdiction over specified international wrongs and rejected claimed service immunity outside United Nations headquarters, leaving factual proof and liability unresolved.

actors.name: Kadic, Doe, and other plaintiffs
actors.role: Alleged victims, relatives, and organizations seeking civil relief

actors.name: Radovan Karadzic
actors.role: President of self-proclaimed Srpska and alleged commander of responsible forces

actors.name: Judge Leisure
actors.role: District judge dismissing for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction

actors.name: Chief Judge Newman
actors.role: Author of the Second Circuit opinion

proceedings: The district court dismissed on the premise that required state action was absent. The Second Circuit reversed and remanded October 13, 1995, then separately denied rehearing in 1996.
limits: The panel established no atrocity liability, final statehood determination, or conclusive disputed service finding. It reserved direct-transit immunity, certain international-law theories, and an independent federal-common-law cause of action. The account states the historical Alien Tort Act ruling.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The complaints alleged an organized campaign of atrocities
sections.cue: Introduce the parties and causes without treating accusations as findings.
paragraphs: Two groups sought civil remedies for alleged atrocities against Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Kadic sued for herself and infant sons; other plaintiffs included victims and women’s organizations. They alleged rape, forced prostitution and impregnation, torture, and summary execution within a campaign to destroy ethnic and religious groups. Radovan Karadzic, president of the self-proclaimed Bosnian-Serb republic Srpska, allegedly commanded the responsible forces.

The suits invoked the Alien Tort Act, 28 U.S.C. section 1350, the Torture Victim Protection Act, general federal-question jurisdiction, and supplemental state claims, seeking compensatory and punitive damages and other relief. Karadzic’s early-1993 visits to New York as a United Nations invitee offered an opportunity for service.

sections.title: New York visits produced two service encounters
sections.cue: Keep the hotel dispute and authorized delivery distinct.
paragraphs: In the Doe action, process servers said they approached Karadzic in the Intercontinental Hotel lobby, announced their purpose, and offered papers from about two feet away. Guards seized them and they fell. A State Department security officer corroborated the encounter but placed the server six feet away.

In Kadic, Judge Owen authorized service through a member of Karadzic’s security detail. An officer said he handed over the complaint outside the Russian Embassy on a later visit, and Karadzic acknowledged receipt. Plaintiffs also alleged he lodged outside United Nations headquarters and conducted unrelated activities including fundraising.

District Judge Leisure nevertheless dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. He understood human-rights liability to require state action, considered Srpska insufficiently established as a state, and treated possible future recognition and head-of-state immunity as reasons against proceeding. He declined supplemental jurisdiction without the further jurisdictional briefing or hearing plaintiffs expected.

sections.title: Not every law-of-nations wrong required a state actor
sections.cue: Explain the genocide and war-crime categories.
paragraphs: Chief Judge Newman, joined by Judges Feinberg and Walker, held that the Alien Tort Act required an alien’s tort claim actually satisfying a treaty or law-of-nations norm, not merely a colorable invocation. Contemporary universally recognized norms governed rather than a frozen 1789 catalogue. Piracy and slave trading historically bound private actors; genocide and war crimes supplied pertinent modern examples. That did not make every private assault an international tort.

Genocide required intent to destroy a protected group wholly or partly. The Genocide Convention expressly covered private people as well as officials. Congress’s criminal implementation disclaimed a new private action but did not implicitly repeal the preexisting Alien Tort Act. Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged destructive intent, subject to proof.

War crimes could also involve nonstate forces. Common article 3 of the Geneva Conventions bound parties to internal conflict and protected those not actively fighting against murder, torture, degrading treatment, hostage-taking, and executions without proper judgment. Organized insurgents did not gain freedom to commit those acts through nonrecognition; commanders’ duties to prevent offenses also mattered. The panel reserved whether Protocol II was universally accepted custom and whether international-conflict rules applied on alternative theories.

sections.title: Other torture claims still required official conduct
sections.cue: Explain the alternative state-action and statutory routes.
paragraphs: Torture and summary execution forming genocide or war crimes could follow those private-actor rules. Independent claims under the norms considered here required official action or color of law. The panel could not yet know whether proof would establish genocidal intent or the armed-conflict link, so those alternatives remained important.

Statehood involved territory, population, government, and capacity for foreign relations; formal recognition was not indispensable. Plaintiffs could try to prove Srpska qualified. Alternatively, they alleged Karadzic acted with recognized former Yugoslav or Serbian officials. Analogies to joint action and substantial state assistance under section 1983 explained possible color of law. The court conclusively determined neither statehood nor those governmental ties.

The Torture Victim Protection Act expressly supplied a remedy for official torture and extrajudicial killing, subject to adequate available local-remedy exhaustion and limitations. It was not itself jurisdictional; section 1350 and general federal-question jurisdiction supplied that foundation. With statutory routes available, the panel reserved whether section 1331 independently supported an implied action for other international norms in federal common law.

sections.title: United Nations invitee status did not bar service outside headquarters
sections.cue: Give the treaty distinctions and limited reservation.
paragraphs: Personal service on an individual physically present ordinarily satisfied service rules and personal-jurisdiction due process. Karadzic invoked the United Nations Headquarters Agreement. Section 9 restricted service inside the defined headquarters district without the Secretary-General’s consent, but these encounters occurred elsewhere. Section 15 protected designated member-state representatives, not an invitee in his position. Section 11 forbade obstacles to invitee transit but did not expressly create general immunity from suit or service. State Department and United Nations legal positions supported that reading.

The panel reserved conceivable protection during direct transit between an entry point and headquarters because he was not served on such a journey. Rules excluding United Nations activities from doing-business jurisdiction calculations did not immunize personal service. Governmental-contact and litigation-related analogies also failed, and speculative future head-of-state recognition did not defeat present jurisdiction.
The immunity conclusion remained conditional on plaintiffs establishing service and their associated allegations. The court did not resolve competing accounts of the hotel encounter as final facts.

sections.title: Foreign-policy implications did not end the suits
sections.cue: State justiciability, the mandate, and rehearing separately.
paragraphs: Applying Baker’s political-question criteria, the panel found manageable international norms and congressional authorization. The Executive affirmatively disclaimed a political-question objection. A contrary position would deserve respectful consideration but not automatically control. Act of state had not been raised below and was not decided; skepticism about applying it to these atrocities was not a holding. Conditions in Bosnia and inadequate Serbia alternatives also left no suitable forum shown for forum-non-conveniens dismissal.
On October 13, 1995, the court reversed the jurisdictional dismissal and remanded, with no separate opinion. Liability, proof, and remaining procedure lay ahead.

At the distinct rehearing stage, Karadzic invoked an article interpreting the 1789 phrase tort only as limited to particular prize-related wrongs. The same panel found that history insufficient against broad statutory language, controlling Filártiga precedent recognizing an international-tort action, and Congress’s later endorsement through the torture statute. A specific historical occasion did not necessarily confine enacted text. The panel denied rehearing at 74 F.3d 377–378 without a separate writing.
